title: How We Built Zeta2: Training an Edit Prediction Model in Production — Ben Kunkle, Zed
talk_summary: Zed trained a small edit-prediction model by distilling a frontier teacher over opt-in production snapshots, with a repair step for bad teacher outputs and a cached JSONL pipeline reusable across experiments. They filter noisy 'settled' user data by sampling many cheap student predictions and keeping examples whose Levenshtein distance to the settled state is in a useful middle band.

takeaways.technique: Heuristic-gated teacher outputs with repair pass
takeaways.what_they_do: Run static heuristics on teacher predictions (e.g., is it just undoing the last edit, does it ignore the editable region), and send failures to a second frontier model with the failure reason to fix before using as training labels.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if it does, then we send it to another frontier model with a similar prompt like, "Hey, it failed in this way. Can you fix it?"

takeaways.technique: Cache the expensive teacher stage, vary only the cheap formatting stage
takeaways.what_they_do: Keep all teacher-generated data in JSONL where each stage adds/moves fields, so the expensive frontier-model labeling is cached and reused across many downstream experiments that only change prompt formatting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: up until that point is reusable across experiments. So, this is stuff that we can cache. We can train multiple experiments on top of that

takeaways.technique: Student model replaces teacher for bulk sampling
takeaways.what_they_do: Once the student approaches teacher quality, use the cheap student checkpoint to generate many samples for filtering instead of the frontier teacher, cutting cost from a million frontier requests to near-zero.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of running the teacher, we can run our student checkpoint or something 50 times. That costs us basically nothing.
takeaways.numbers: 100,000 examples would need ~1,000,000 frontier requests; student sampling is 'basically nothing'

takeaways.technique: Distance-band filtering of noisy ground truth
takeaways.what_they_do: Compare candidate outputs to the eventual settled state via Levenshtein/n-gram distance; discard far-away (noise) and trivially-close (obvious) cases, keep the middle band as the most informative examples.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's this interesting section in the middle where it's almost. That's like the ideal what we want in our training examples.

takeaways.technique: Multiple reference answers for no-single-answer tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: Evaluate against three distinct teacher predictions rather than one gold answer, since many tasks have multiple valid outputs; being close to any one counts as good.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're generally running against three teacher predictions cuz a lot of these have no one right answer.

takeaways.technique: Diagnostic-count delta as a quality signal
takeaways.what_they_do: Snapshot error/diagnostic counts before and after a prediction and use the delta as a proxy for output quality.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We snapshot how many errors there are before the prediction, how many there are after. And then we're and try and use that to judge the quality of the model.
